item.title: I have some criticism
item.content:encoded: I am a researcher of railway history and I have some criticism for this tale. This story appears to take place during the American Civil War, a very interesting time in American railroad history. However, I was perplexed as to why there was twisted metal, much less a metal boxcar. At the time, most coaches and freight cars were wood. Actually, scratch that. All train cars were wood at the time. The only exception would be the armored battle trains used during the civil war. Metal train cars didn’t become standard until after the great train wreck of 1917, where 101 people were killed in a head on collision. Now, I’m not blaming you. The SCP Foundation wiki is known to have very inaccurate and false representations of railroads. Also, train cars are not called cabs. For cars carrying freight, call them either freight cars or rolling stock. As for passengers, call them passenger cars or coaches. Only use the word cab when referring to the cab of a locomotive, which is where the engineer and fireman operate the train. I hope I didn’t sound to condescending. I know that most people know little to nothing about trains, so I’m not going to be angry when people get things wrong. Aside from everything I’ve mentioned, I really do like this tale! Well done!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Your prose is clumsy and unwieldy. Lines like

The polite silence of a group of people comfortable in each other's existence but unwilling to initiate conversation suffocated the first 10 cabs.

are overwrought and poorly structured, while lines like

Knight ribbed him as they both grabbed their pistols from the gun cabinet in the corner of the metal boxcar.

feel unnecessary and redundant, particularly given the context of their preceding or following lines. Most of the writing is short and choppy, but then you occasionally lob complex language bombs into the writing in an attempt to gussy it up, which ends up backfiring. For example, the first line I quoted is part of this passage:

"Inside the cars, things were quiet. The polite silence of a group of people comfortable in each other's existence but unwilling to initiate conversation suffocated the first 10 cabs."

The first sentence makes the second redundant. Even if the second sentence is an attempt to enhance the atmosphere of the piece, its clumsiness and deluge of prepositions ruins the attempt.

The general clumsiness of your prose ruins the voice and mood you're trying to go for. You're trying to style on the English language but not committing to it, which makes the narrator's voice inconsistent and pulls me out of the experience. The biggest issue you have is your inconsistency. But it's fixable.

If you want to comment on the morals of people on the train, that needs one voice. If you want to tell a more action-packed story that's another voice. But you can't mix and match them. Pick which you think is more important and stick with it. Either decide you want to do a literary commentary on morals, and stick to that and forgo the action; or decide you want to make it more fast-paced, and don't worry about commenting on social morals.

Once you find a consistent voice, things should go much smoother. The wording and sentence structure are eminently fixable, and are close to being good - it's simply a matter of picking how you want to say your story and sticking with it.

item.content:encoded:
They miss the whisper that runs
any day in your mind,
“Who are you really, wanderer?”—

and the answer you have to give
no matter how dark and cold
the world around you is:
“Maybe I’m a king.”

-William Stafford

Betcha weren't expecting that. At least I hope you weren't. Thanks to Doctor Cimmerian, RockTeethMothEyes, DrChandra, OthellotheCat, and Uncle Nicolini for feedback, and a special thanks to Cimmerian for creating the Aces and Eights canon this takes place in.
